# Improving Generalization Robustness of Multimodal RLVR

- **Authors**: Pengfei Zhou, Zhiwei Tang, Xiaopeng Peng, Chenrui Zhou, Lama Moukheiber, Yixing Ma, Bin Xu, Jiajun Song, Zhenglin Wan, Wangbo Zhao, Jiasheng Tang, Bohan Zhuang, Fan Wang, Yang You
- **Venue**: cs.AI
- **Published**: 2026-08-09
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08802>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08802v1>
- **Topics**: reasoning-training
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-training 0.62

## In one line

Traces the brittleness of multimodal RLVR gains under paraphrase and template change to two properties of the standard objective -- a binary verifier that cannot distinguish a wrong answer from a misformatted one, and a training distribution covering a thin slice of the prompts a deployed model meets -- and fixes both with a trinary reward and an invariance penalty across semantically equivalent prompts.

## Problem

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards makes multimodal models more accurate, but the gains do not survive rewording: paraphrasing a question or changing the prompt template degrades them, which matters most in exactly the domains where such systems are proposed for deployment. Two properties of the standard objective are identified as causes. The binary verifier conflates format with content, so the reward cannot separate an answer that is wrong from one that is merely formatted differently, and the policy has no way to learn which it is being punished for. And the training distribution covers only a narrow band of the semantically equivalent prompts the model will encounter, so a policy that does well on that band can behave differently outside it.

## Contributions

- A diagnosis of RLVR brittleness in two specific properties of the objective: a binary verifier that conflates format with content so the policy cannot tell which error it is being punished for, and a training prompt distribution too narrow to cover deployment-time phrasings.
- A dynamic trinary reward separating format from semantics, and a consistency regulariser enforcing policy invariance across meaning-preserving prompt perturbations generated by an embedding-space adversary.
- A separation of template stress -- rewording that leaves the task intact -- from operator-based mutations that change the task, with the observation that only the former tests prompt robustness and the honest consequence that two of the paper's own evaluations do not support its central claim.
- A template-count sweep showing that standard RLVR's in-distribution accuracy itself degrades as the evaluation template set grows, so the brittleness is not confined to out-of-distribution prompts.
- A comparison against multi-template training rather than only against single-template GRPO, which isolates the invariance constraint from mere exposure to prompt variety.
- An ablation reported as inconclusive where it is, with the components presented as principled additions of no detectable cost rather than as necessary, and an unfavourable dynamic-test number explained by its own mechanism rather than omitted.

## Method

Two corresponding interventions. A dynamic trinary reward replaces the binary verifier so that format and semantics are separated in the signal rather than collapsed into one bit. A consistency regulariser then enforces policy invariance across perturbations that preserve meaning, with the perturbations generated by an embedding-space adversary that edits the instruction side only -- image-side robustness is reported separately. Evaluation is deliberately two-tiered and the paper distinguishes the tiers carefully. A template stress test swaps the prompt template while leaving the task intact, which is the rewording failure the method targets. A dynamic test applies operator-based input mutations, some of which do not preserve the task at all -- multiple-choice questions reconstructed into free-form question answering, and document layouts mutated -- and the paper flags these as task-altering rather than as paraphrase. Baselines are standard GRPO and a multi-template GRPO variant trained on five templates, which is the fair comparison since it also sees prompt variety without the invariance constraint. Evaluation spans general examination visual question answering plus two deployment-oriented domains, medical and legal, on two base models, with results averaged over three seeds and an explicit inconclusive threshold of about 1.5 points against which individual comparisons are judged.

## Results

Under template stress the standard objective loses what it gained: on one backbone it drops 4.4 points on a mathematics benchmark, 2.3 and 6.7 on two medical sets, and 2.4 on the legal set, while the proposed method is flat to positive on all four (+0.3, +0.8, -0.8, +0.2) and matches or beats the multi-template baseline. Averaged over benchmarks, the drop under stress is at most 1 percent against roughly 3 percent for standard GRPO. The template-count sweep shows the mechanism: standard GRPO's in-distribution accuracy itself falls from 49.5 at one template to 47.7 at five or more, the multi-template variant flattens that at 49.5 in-distribution and 32.3 out, and the invariance-trained policy holds 51.1 in-distribution while its out-of-distribution accuracy rises with the number of templates. Under the dynamic test the picture is more mixed and the paper says so. On medical question answering it is consistently the least-degraded trained method (-7.3 against -12.1, -3.1 against -5.8, -7.2 against -7.6), but on the multiple-choice mathematics set every method collapses by 47 to 49 points because the mutation reconstructs multiple choice into free-form answering, and on the legal set every method loses about 20 points to document-layout mutation. The authors draw the right conclusion from this rather than reporting the aggregate: those are task-altering mutations rather than rewordings, so the prompt-robustness claim rests on the template stress test and not on them. The ablation is reported as inconclusive where it is inconclusive. The full method has the strongest stress result (+0.6 against GRPO's -2.3), but the multi-template-plus-trinary-reward configuration sits at 0.0, within noise of it, so the authors state the ablation does not cleanly isolate the individual contributions of the trinary reward or the adversary beyond multi-template training, and present those two as principled additions with no detectable cost rather than as individually necessary. They also explain an unfavourable number rather than omitting it -- on one benchmark their dynamic drop is worse than GRPO's because their higher standard accuracy enlarges the absolute fall -- and note one medical comparison that fails to clear their own inconclusive threshold. On pass@8 the method is flat against the untrained base and 0.6 to 2.5 points above GRPO, which the authors read as consistent with evidence that RLVR reweights existing probability mass rather than enlarging the reasoning frontier.

## Limitations

Stated throughout rather than in one section, and unusually candidly. The ablation cannot separate the trinary reward or the adversary from multi-template training, and the authors decline to claim they are individually necessary. One high-stakes comparison does not clear their own stated 1.5-point inconclusive threshold and is reported as not clearing it. The dynamic-test aggregate is described as dominated by a benchmark on which every method collapses, so it cannot separate components. Two of the dynamic mutations are identified as task-altering rather than paraphrase, which removes them from supporting the paper's central claim. The theoretical proposition offered as a mechanism is explicitly said not to be a fitted prediction of the observed curve. The adversary edits only the instruction side. Not stated but worth noticing: the robustness gain is measured against templates and mutations the authors constructed, so 'invariance to semantically equivalent prompts' means invariance to their perturbation family, and an adversary trained in embedding space optimises against the same representation the invariance is enforced over. Pass@8 being flat against the base means the method improves robustness of what the base could already do rather than extending it, which the authors state plainly.

## Why it matters here

- **reasoning-training**: Two contributions, one substantive and one methodological, and the methodological one is the better. Substantively, the paper isolates a cost of binary verifiable rewards the archive had not recorded: a single bit cannot distinguish a wrong answer from a differently-formatted one, so the policy learns format and content together and neither cleanly -- which is the same collapse-into-one-signal problem the archive holds elsewhere in the form of a tolerance threshold serving two purposes, and the fix has the same shape, splitting the signal rather than tuning it. The accompanying measurement is worth keeping on its own: standard RLVR's in-distribution accuracy drops from 49.5 to 47.7 as the evaluation template set grows from one to five, so brittleness is not only an out-of-distribution phenomenon and a single-template evaluation overstates what training achieved. Methodologically, this is one of the more disciplined papers in the archive about what its own evidence supports. It separates rewording from task alteration and then rules two of its own evaluations out of its central claim on that basis, because a mutation that turns multiple choice into free-form answering or scrambles a document layout is not a paraphrase and every method losing 20 to 49 points on it measures something else. It states an inconclusive threshold in advance and reports which of its comparisons fail to clear it. It explains an unfavourable number by its own mechanism rather than dropping it. And its ablation concludes that two of its three components cannot be separated from the third, so they are presented as principled additions with no detectable cost rather than as necessary -- which is the correct reading of an ablation that clusters within noise and is rarely the one given. Finally, the pass@8 result places the work inside the archive's existing position: flat against the untrained base, above GRPO, and read by the authors themselves as consistent with RLVR reweighting existing probability mass rather than enlarging the frontier. So robustness here is robustness of access to what the base model could already do.

## Abstract

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) makes Multimodal Large Language Models more accurate, but the gains are brittle: simply paraphrasing a question or changing the prompt template can degrade them, which challenges reliable deployment in high-stakes scenarios like medical VQA. We trace this to two issues of the standard RL objective. First, the binary verifier conflates format with content, so the reward signal cannot tell a wrong answer apart from a misformatted one. Second, the training distribution covers only a thin slice of the real-world prompts that the model might meet at deployment, so policies that perform well on the training distribution can behave differently under unseen prompts during test. Both failures call for a robust post-training method that helps the policy cover a broader distribution of semantically equivalent prompts, and we identify two measures that help achieve this objective: separating format from semantics in the reward, and applying policy invariance across perturbed prompts with equivalent semantics. We therefore propose Prompt-Invariant RLVR (PIRL), consisting of a dynamic trinary reward and a consistency regularizer based on an embedding-space adversary. Under stress testing, PIRL's average accuracy on benchmarks drops by only $\le 1\%$, where GRPO drops ~3%. On dynamic evaluation, PIRL also achieves the smallest performance drop.
